audio_track_actual: Narrator voiceover over archival audio from 9/11-truth video material. Includes excerpted audio from Lorne Lyles describing CeCe Lyles' calls from UA Flight 93.
video_overlay_text_observed: Opening title: 'WHAT REALLY HAPPENED ON 9/11? (The Disgusting Truth) — part 46/56.' On-screen: photo of CeCe Lyles. Subsequent frames show photos of Thomas Burnett, Jeremy Glick, Ted Olson.
audio_content_summary: Argues that the cell-phone calls reported from 9/11 flights are forensically suspicious. Specific claims: (1) Audio from Lorne Lyles' answering-machine recording of CeCe Lyles' call from UA93 is 'too clean' — no engine/cabin background noise. (2) CeCe Lyles' call at 9:47 a.m. was from cell phone (per caller ID), at ~20,000 ft, which the narrator claims is technically impossible. (3) Deena Burnett (Thomas Burnett's wife) said caller ID showed her husband's cell number — also UA93. (4) Lyzbeth Glick (Jeremy Glick's wife) testified in deposition that the call connection was 'very clear, as if he was calling from the next room.' (5) Theodore Olson, then Solicitor General, originally said his wife Barbara Olson (AA77) called him from a cell phone, then later changed his account to air phones. (6) Olson in 2002 argued Christopher v. Harbury at SCOTUS that 'the government has [an] inherent right' / 'legitimate reasons to give out false information.'
implied_frame: The 9/11 cellphone calls from the planes were fabricated; therefore the official narrative is false. (Mixed Group B / C. The specific factual hooks — Lyles' call, Deena Burnett's account, Glick's wife's deposition, Olson's account changing — are real and on the record. The technical claim that cell phones could not connect from a plane at altitude is contested: NIST/AT&T/Verizon technical analyses confirmed connections at low altitudes are possible, calls from UA93 at altitudes below ~20k ft and during descent are technically feasible, and the dropped/clear-audio mix matches expected RF behavior. The narrator's quote-pull from Olson's Christopher v. Harbury SCOTUS argument needs context: Olson was arguing the narrow point that government officials are not always liable for misrepresentations in the course of duty, not that the government has a general 'right to lie.')
